claims.text: The Z method is an efficient alternative to full thermodynamic integration for calculating melting properties of high-melting refractory materials.
The Z method can calculate melting temperature, latent heat, entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
The material begins in a crystalline solid state.
The Z-method simulation uses ab initio molecular dynamics in the microcanonical NVE ensemble.
The simulation starts from an overheated solid and proceeds until spontaneous melting occurs.
The simulations are conducted at constant energy and volume near the expected melting point.
A solid-liquid coexistence region emerges within the simulation cell.
Spontaneous melting of the superheated solid causes a sudden change in energy.
Spontaneous melting under the stated conditions causes a sudden change in volume.
The sudden transition permits extraction of melting temperature, enthalpy change, entropy change, and volume change without extensive free-energy integration.
Z-method melting properties will closely match results from ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The Z method has significantly lower computational cost than ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The reduced computational cost will enable high-throughput screening of refractory materials.
The approach is expected to be valid for high-melting materials with a well-defined phase change.
Simulation cell size and simulation duration affect accurate capture of phase coexistence dynamics.
Complex melting mechanisms or significant metastability may limit the approach.
The quantitative accuracy of Z-method fusion enthalpy and entropy may be lower than that of full free-energy integration.

contradictions.description: The intervention and conditions specify a constant-volume NVE simulation, while the mechanism invokes a sudden change in volume during that same transition.

The mechanism claims that volume change at melting can be extracted directly from a transition conducted at fixed volume, without specifying additional simulations, pressure information, or an equation-of-state procedure.
